title: The 1997-1999 fall in runoff at equal rain was not global: it went away in Germany and Great Britain, and only former East Germany fell as much as south-east Australia, from about 1992
abstract: Question: after 1997, runoff in south-east Australia (SE-AU) and, with no drought, in the eastern US fell below the earlier rainfall-runoff relation. Did one global cause make this change? If so, other mid-latitude regions with gauge-based rain must show the same fall. Approach: one annual model, sqrt(Q) = a + bP + cP(t-1), fitted on 1971-1996 per catchment, for 1,642 catchments in seven regions: CAMELS-AUS (AGCD), US (nClimGrid), CAMELS-DE (HYRAS, 1952-2020) and CAMELS-GB (CEH-GEAR, 1971-2015). Plan and decision rule were written before any German or British result. Results: mean standardized departures in 1997-2009 and 2010-end were -0.88 and -0.88 SD in SE-AU, -0.47 and -0.57 in the eastern US, -0.33 and -0.14 [-0.41, +0.06] in Germany (no drop by the rule; inside earlier 13-year block variation) and -0.56 and -0.11 in Great Britain (unresolved; P2 has 6 years). So the global synchronous drop is not supported. The best common step year was 1998 in SE-AU and 1999 in the eastern US, but 1990 in Germany, at the time of the 1988-1989 European temperature rise. Temperature removed the small German P2 departure but only 17% of the SE-AU one; VPD removed none. Post hoc, Germany split at the former inner-German border: 284 former-West catchments were at +0.01 SD in 2010-2020, but 50 former-East catchments were at -1.06 SD (about -17% of flow, best step 1992), in forested and farmed catchments alike. Within 25 km of the border, 90% of eastern catchments were negative (median -15%) against a western median of -3%. Near the border, eastern rain rose 6 points relative to the west after 1993, also at fixed DWD stations with unchanged Hellmann gauges (+5.1, 95% CI 3.4-6.8). Eastern flow fell 9 points, so the change is not a rain-gridding artifact. Conclusion: the persistent SE-AU loss is not part of one global change. Germany and Great Britain had a 1997-2009 low that went away. A persistent fall of SE-AU size occurred only in former East Germany, and it follows a political border, so its cause is most probably connected with reunification, not climate. Limitations: one annual model; intervals do not include shared year noise; GB ends in 2015; the East German analysis is post hoc with 50 catchments; causes in East Germany were not tested.
